articles.title: Horned dinosaurs' weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat
articles.text:
Horned dinosaurs' weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat
Skip to content
Subscribe today
Every print subscription comes with full digital access
Subscribe Now
By Jake Buehler
October 16, 2026 at 11:00 am
Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)
Email
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.
New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.
Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.
Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.
Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.
Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.
Researchers simulated the stresses on the ceratopsians’ skulls under different fighting behaviors. For example, on the Triceratops skull, the team simulated forces from a single horn stabbing (left), horns interlocking a quarter of the way up the shaft (middle), and horns locked at an angle (right).E.A. Ames, A.J. Rowe and D.J. Button/PeerJ, 2026, 3-D Model Courtesy of the Smithsonian Institution (Copyright: Smithsonian Institution)
The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species  like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.
Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.
Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”
Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”
The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.

articles.title: Artemis II results show how much science people can do at the moon
articles.text:
Artemis II results show how much science people can do at the moon
Skip to content
Subscribe today

Subscribe Now
By Lisa Grossman
October 16, 2026 at 9:00 am
Share this:
Share

Email

Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
Six months after the Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon, the value of their closeup view is coming into focus. The first science results, released on October 7, reveal details of the moon’s array of colors, how often it gets hit by tiny rocks and lessons for squeezing as much science as possible out of future human lunar missions.
“We worked extremely hard to make sure we were able to maximize lunar science return from wherever we could in this mission,” said Artemis II flight science operations lead Kelsey Young at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting on October 7. “This is creating yet another tool in our toolbox as planetary scientists to understand our moon, our solar system, even our own planet.”
NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon in April — the first time humans had been anywhere near our natural satellite in more than 50 years. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen spent about seven hours in close proximity to the moon taking scientific observations, describing the moon’s surprising colors and textures and witnessing a solar eclipse from space.
Almost all of that event was livestreamed. But the astronauts took thousands of photos, notes and audio recordings that weren’t immediately made public. Part of the science team’s job was to digest those observations and release the data to anyone who wants to study them within six months of splashdown on April 10.
With three days to spare, the team released three reports and a massive data archive on October 7, the 67th anniversary of when the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft took the first photograph of the farside of the moon. The results offer a rare test of what trained human observers can add to lunar research and what NASA can learn for future missions to the lunar surface.
“We’re really excited to release all of this data,” earth scientist Sara Schmidt of NASA Johnson Space flight Cener in Houston said during the meeting. After six months of hard work, “this is enabling science to happen for the next, I don’t know, 60 years, if not more.”
How astronauts learn to observe the moon
Surprisingly, the most valuable data from the mission were not the mind-blowingly gorgeous photos, but the astronauts’ verbal and written descriptions of what they were seeing.
Before launch, the astronauts had extensive training in lunar geology and science observations. They were an extension of the science team, said field geologist Cindy Evans also of NASA Johnson Space Flight Center, one of the astronauts’ instructors.
“You could hear it in their voices. They understood the language of geology,” she said.
That training was meant to help answer a question Young hears often: What can humans add that a camera can’t?
During the flyby, the astronauts worked in pairs. Two of them spoke to mission control on the ground, giving periodic updates to the science team on what they were seeing. The other two recorded themselves describing their observations and reactions and used a stylus to annotate specially made maps of the moon that had been uploaded to their tablets during flight. Those notes, doodles and recordings were not made public until now.
The idea was to give the crew high tech field notebooks, Young says.
“If you have any field experience, you know your field notebook is your best friend,” she said in the meeting. On Earth, geologists capture nuance and context in written and spoken words, as well as sketches, she said. “We wanted to provide the ability to capture that nuanced information from the crew.”
One example of this was when Koch sketched her view of the Orientale basin, detailing differences in texture and layers around the crater.
“Sketches can be so powerful,” Young says. “They’re quick and dirty and that’s exactly the right thing to do. You’re capturing that nuance really quickly before it leaves your brain.”
NASA astronaut Christina Koch made a quick sketch of the Orientale basin during the lunar flyby on April 6 to describe differences in texture and layering. The moon’s south pole is at the top of the image.NASA
Some of the most unique observations came during the 54 minutes when the moon eclipsed the sun, giving the astronauts a view of the solar corona, interplanetary dust and other stars and planets. That was a favorite moment for planetary scientist Jennifer Heldmann of NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.
“That audio showed their sheer joy and amazement in what they were seeing and where they were,” Heldmann says. “They were so blown away by what they were seeing, while also taking very relevant science observations.”
But some of the most affecting moments were when words failed. When Glover and Koch saw the Earth emerge from behind the moon, for a while all they could say was “Oh my gosh!”
“I guess I should be trying to describe it, but I mean, good grief,” Glover’s tablet recorded him saying.
“No, I tried, but it’s impossible,” Koch agreed. “You might be able to fly a spaceship and talk, but if you can see that and talk, you just ain’t right.”
Astronauts spotted tiny impacts on the moon
Another thing the astronauts were able to see during the eclipse were impact flashes — tiny blips of light marking where bits of rock hit the moon.
“It’s a pinpoint of light,” Hansen said in his recorded observations. “It’s not like a meteor, you didn’t see anything else, it’s just like a bloop.”

Many American diets may not include enough of this essential nutrient

Share this:

Grocery store shelves are bursting with fancy salts: Himalayan, kosher, sea salt and more. Considering these choices, it can be easy to forget about the public health victory found in basic, iodized table salt.
The nutrient iodine is a crucial component of thyroid hormones, necessary for fetal and early childhood brain development and health throughout life. At the start of the last century, iodine deficiency was a rampant and visible public health problem in the United States, with the telltale sign of enlarged thyroid glands, called goiters, especially prevalent in much of the north. A series of steps taken by a medical society in Michigan and U.S. salt producers brought iodized salt to tables across the country, and by the 1950s, occurrences of goiters had dropped precipitously.
But more recently, the United States appears to be backsliding on iodine nutrition. In 2017 and 2018, 24 percent of women and 30 percent of men, aged 14 and older, weren’t getting an adequate amount of the nutrient. That’s about twice as many as in 2001 and 2002, researchers reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2025. Breaking the data down further, nearly half of pregnant women haven’t been getting enough iodine. The study reflects an estimated, short-term look at population iodine levels.
Long-term, a consistent dearth of iodine robs the body of the ability to produce sufficient amounts of thyroid hormones. If iodine levels in the population continue to trend down, that could eventually result in more goiters and harm brain development in children.
“The group that has the most severe potential consequences of iodine deficiency is pregnant women,” says Elizabeth Pearce, an endocrinologist at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine. “Even mild degrees of iodine deficiency in pregnancy may be associated with measurably lower IQ in children.”
Yet women of reproductive age, at the U.S. population level, are on the cusp of mild iodine deficiency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated in its 2026 Nutrition Report.
With all of the ways that diets, salt intake and noniodized options have changed over time, the importance of iodine nutrition may not be top-of-mind for the general public like it was a century ago. “Iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide of preventable developmental delay,” says Monica Serrano-Gonzalez, a pediatric endocrinologist at Hasbro Children’s and Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School in Providence, R.I. “People have kind of forgotten this is a risk.”
The “goiter belt”
When iodine deficiency keeps the thyroid gland from making enough hormones, the body calls for more, which stimulates and enlarges the gland. That supersized gland, called a goiter, bulges at the neck. In the United States, goiters were extremely common a century ago in the Northwest, Great Lakes and Appalachians; together, the area became known as the “goiter belt.” Iodine naturally occurs in seawater and soil. But in the noncoastal northern part of the country, soils and water sources have little iodine, so the crops produced in these inland areas lack the nutrient.
An examining physician for the World War I draft reported in 1918 that 30 percent of almost 600 men from a northern Michigan county had goiters, some large enough to be disqualifying. A 1922 Michigan Department of Health study of schoolchildren in four counties revealed that close to 50 percent had goiters. “It would have been a really visible public health problem at that time,” Pearce says.
In response to the state’s iodine issues, the Michigan State Medical Society recommended the addition of the nutrient to table salt. The minimal expense for iodization meant this common kitchen staple would remain affordable. Companies introduced iodized salt in Michigan in the spring of 1924. By the fall, the Morton Salt Company, a major producer, was selling iodized salt nationwide. Over time, the goiters of the “belt” dwindled.
Salt iodization has been linked to rising IQ in the United States. For example, for men born in areas without natural sources of iodine, there was a significant jump in World War II Air Force acceptances, based on a qualifying exam, after widespread salt iodization. The increase did not occur among men born in areas with adequate natural sources of the nutrient, researchers reported in the Journal of the European Economic Association in 2017.
Adding iodine to salt was never mandated by the U.S. government. But for a long time, the voluntary approach — combined with how most people consumed salt and other dietary habits — did the trick to get people enough iodine. Today, different meal practices and available food options are tearing holes in the iodine safety net. “Iodized salt is important, but it may not be reaching everybody anymore,” Pearce says.
There are many more noniodized salt options today, with one analysis reporting that only 53 percent of table salt sold in U.S. stores is iodized. People get much of their salt from prepared, processed and packaged foods, which generally are made with noniodized salt. Milk can provide iodine, due to iodine-supplemented feed and the use of an iodine cleanser on cows’ udders. But the amount of iodine in milk can vary greatly, a recent analysis found, probably because industry practices can differ. Diets that restrict dairy may also put people at risk of consuming too little iodine.
The U.S. recommended dietary allowance for iodine for adults is 150 micrograms per day, which rises to 220 mcg for pregnant people and 290

A new set of remains found in modern-day Iraq suggests that one Neandertal probably suffered a devastating blow to the face before dying at the point of a spear many years later.
The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write October 15 in Scientific Reports. But violence isn’t all this Neandertal may have known. A shattered tooth found with the remains hints that the deceased suffered a facial injury at some point in their life. Surviving this injury indicates that Neandertals may have helped each other in times of need, the study authors speculate.
These remains with visible trauma are “super cool,” because “there’s a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton,” says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri in Columbia who wasn’t involved with the study.
Neandertals were often injured throughout their lives, probably from hunting. But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids — modern humans and their extinct cousins — were stabbing and pummeling each other, maybe even intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago. Signs of injuries caused by other hominids have included another Neandertal at the same Iraq site whose rib was probably stabbed.
During an excavation that began in 2019 at Shanidar, the famous Neandertal burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, researchers uncovered remains from at least three previously unknown individuals. The set included ribs, hand bones, teeth and a perforated shoulder bone that probably belonged to a single individual who lived around 75,000 years ago.
At first, the team had no idea what caused the hole, says Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It’s so round, it’s like, what is it?” she recalls thinking at the time.
The team removed the shoulder blade with the surrounding sediment and tested for evidence that roots or insects had damaged the fossil. But that didn’t fit the nature of the damage.
Instead, they found fragments of bone from the shoulder blade in the dirt that suggested it had been pierced when the individual, which the team named Shanidar A, was alive. The team also didn’t see any signs of healing around the puncture wound when they analyzed the bone under the microscope and using X-rays — suggesting that the injury had occurred around the time of death.
The next task was to find out what instrument might have caused the injury. The team compared the puncture with the fossilized remains of butchered animals found alongside human tools, as well as wounds created by archaeologists stabbing animal corpses with re-created Paleolithic weapons. Stone-tipped spears usually create a diamond-shaped hole. Wooden spears, on the other hand, tend to leave round puncture wounds.
The wound was “absolutely, without any question,” made by a wooden spear, says Bruno Maureille, an anthropologist at the University of Bordeaux in France who wasn’t on the study team.
Shanidar A’s tooth broke due to a bad injury. The Neandertal may have received some help from others in its group after the incident.Emma Pomeroy
The team also found a broken incisor alongside the rest of the remains. The tooth was so shattered that Shanidar A probably experienced a serious injury to their face. Tartar buildup suggests that the tooth splintered in half years before Shanidar A died, meaning they lived with their disability for a long time.
“Given it would have affected their ability to eat, to drink — they’d have been in massive amount of pain at first — it’s likely [to] have needed some care,” Pomeroy says. That one set of remains suggest both violence and care show that Neandertal “behavior is complex,” Pomeroy says. “Like us.”

On paper, my interview with Casey Harrell looks like any other.
I ask the questions, he answers them. He tells me about his background as a climate activist, his Southern roots and his daughter, who as a preschooler loved to dress up like a cheetah and roar around the house. “My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit,” Harrell says.
The transcript tells the story of our conversation. But between the lines is an entirely different story — the story of where Harrell’s words come from.
Harrell started losing his ability to speak in his early 40s, nearly six years ago. He talked to me using a brain implant that can decode his words directly from his thoughts. The device, called a brain-computer interface, is experimental. But it has transformed Harrell’s life. And it could soon transform others. Advances in computing power and AI, lessons gleaned from patient experience and investments from neurotechnology companies are starting to yield real progress on brain-computer interfaces for people who can no longer talk. In other words, Harrell’s new voice might not be so singular in the future.
After Casey Harrell gets out of bed in the morning, he plugs into the Matrix, as he puts it. The elaborate and experimental system lets Harrell speak, an ability that ALS stole from him.Regents of the Univ. of California, Davis
“There’s a lot of excitement and hope in the field right now,” says Matthew Willsey, a neuro­surgeon and biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, who recently implanted a new type of speech interface in a woman’s brain. For years, Willsey says, scientists didn’t know whether attempts to decode speech would be successful; now, a body of research results points clearly to yes. “They’re thinking, ‘Wow, this is actually a usable technology that addresses a real problem that people suffer from.’”
Harrell has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. The progressive neurodegenerative disease, which affects an estimated 35,000 people in the United States, kills nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscles. As the neural connections between Harrell’s brain and body began to falter, he gradually lost his ability to move his muscles, leaving him confined to his bed or a wheelchair. Some of those dropped signals directed the muscles in his throat and mouth, the ones that allow him to speak.
“I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020,” Harrell says. After that, it was “a slow-motion car crash” as fewer and fewer people could understand him. “[My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease,” he says.
In a stroke of luck, Harrell learned through a family member about a clinical trial happening at the University of California, Davis — one that attempted to restore speech with a brain-computer interface. In 2023, Harrell had four small devices implanted on the left side of his brain. These grids of electrodes reside on Harrell’s speech motor cortex, a stretch of brain along the precentral gyrus that controls the movements required for speech.
Today, Harrell uses his system for about 10 to 14 hours daily, making him, as he puts it, “the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.” Hard data suggest he’s right. A recent count shows that Harrell has used his system to communicate nearly 2 million words, the scientists working with him reported in June in Nature Medicine.
“I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020 … [My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease.” Casey Harrell
The very existence of Harrell’s words shows it may be possible to restore speech for people with ALS, as well as for those whose speech is impaired by stroke, paralysis, cerebral palsy and Parkinson’s disease. “This kind of technology has the potential to dramatically change the conversation,” says David Brandman, a UC Davis neurosurgeon and neuroscientist who works with Harrell.
Harrell’s interface still has room for improvement. It’s bulky, relatively slow and limited in what sorts of nonword sounds it can decode.
But it is a “beginning,” says Leigh Hochberg, a neuroscientist at Brown University who works with Harrell. “It’s still early days. There’s a lot of research to happen, and it’s going to be very exciting.” The end game, Hochberg says, is a world in which people could use a device to communicate seamlessly, quickly, clearly — and in their former voices.
Success would mean restoring more than just people’s words, Brandman says. It would mean restoring their ability to connect in all the ineffable ways that make us human. “Speech is so fundamental to who we are,” he says. “Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”
The voice inside
On the path to a technology that enables fast, natural speech, scientists first had to answer a more basic question: Could the brain’s electrical chatter be decoded and translated into action outside of the head?
Nerve cells speak to each other with tiny pulses of electricity, signals that can be picked up with electrodes. The existence of this electrical language raised the tantalizing idea that electrical messages could be decoded straight from where they originate in the brain, bypassing damaged links to the rest of the body.
“This has

articles.title: Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other
articles.text:
Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other
Skip to content

By Brendan Pierson

Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)

Facebook

Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
Medical implants are getting smaller and smarter. But getting them to talk to each other remains tricky.
Now, researchers have developed a way for tiny implantable devices to send electrical signals through the body’s own tissues. The approach could offer a low-power way for implants to work together, with one detecting a symptom and another delivering treatment, the team reports September 24 in Science.
Currently, getting devices to communicate through tissue comes with trade-offs. Some medical devices, such as insulin pumps linked to glucose monitors, use Bluetooth, which relies on radio signals. Receiving those signals requires power even when a device is only listening, increasing the need for battery power and making devices harder shrink. Radio signals also weaken as they travel through body tissue, limiting how far apart communicating devices can be.
The new network called SWANS, the Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, works differently. A wearable external hub or implant generates an electric pulse that produces a small current in the surrounding tissue. Tiny implants can detect those electrical signals while using almost no power when they are only listening. And without large batteries, those implants can be small enough to inject through a syringe.
To demonstrate how the network works, the team attached motion sensors to the front legs of rats. When the animals moved their front legs, the system’s external hub sent signals through their bodies to neurostimulator implants in the sciatic nerves, causing muscles in the back legs to contract.
The synchronized limbs weren’t really the point. The experiment was designed to show that signals could travel through the body, linking different kinds of devices, says Alex Abramson, a biomedical engineer at Georgia Tech in Atlanta. It was “a proof of concept showing that you can really connect this system to anything.”
Abramson says a network of smart implants could automatically deliver a drug or stimulate a neuron exactly when needed to treat complex conditions like Parkinson’s disease. Simple signals can be sent from one implant to another, while an external hub can coordinate more complex networks of sensors and devices, possibly using artificial intelligence.
Before the new network can be used in humans, researchers will need to show that the electrical signals do not cause unintended problems like heart rhythm disruptions. Such issues  have not turned up in the experiments in rats yet, but the technology will need to be tested over longer periods of time and in larger animals, Abramson says.
Materials engineer Amir Alavi says the network’s potential could grow as other technologies improve, including wearables, AI systems and miniature, battery-free implantable sensors like those his lab is developing. “There are now several really interesting directions converging,” says Alavi, of at the University of Pittsburgh’s Swanson School of Engineering. “If those pieces eventually come together, you could have implants that are much smaller, simpler, longer-lived, and more connected than what we have today.”

Four ancient footprints are helping scientists step into a T. rex’s shoes.
The prints form the  first set of tracks probably left behind by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex, researchers report September 8 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Measurements of the 7-meter-long trackway suggest the  ancient predator was ambling along at about 1.6 meters per second, roughly equivalent to a person’s quick walking pace.
A few single adult T. rex footprints exist in the fossil record, as do trackways possibly from T. rex juveniles or  other dinosaur species, says Peter Falkingham, a paleontologist at Liverpool John Moores University in England. “But an individual track doesn’t tell you a lot. A trackway tells you more about foot placement as the animal’s moving along.” And younger and older dinosaurs probably walked differently, just as human toddlers and adults do.
“Finding an adult trackway is cool,” Falkingham says. “It’s unique. It brings something new.”
High school teacher and paleontologist Kent Hups stumbled on the footprints in 2025, while fossil hunting along a steep incline in the Hell Creek Formation in North Dakota. The tracks stick up out of the ground because sediment filled in the originally muddy footprints, which then eroded away more slowly than the surrounding rock.
When Hups saw the first track, he noted that it was three-toed and enormous, measuring 80 centimeters across. “I’m going, ‘this has to be a T. rex,’” says Hups, of Northglenn High School in Colo. and the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
Four Tyrannosaurus rex footprints, shown from above in a drone photo (left), make up the first discovered trackway left behind by an adult. The frontmost footprint (right) is the best preserved and has three distinct toes.K. Hups
Slender toe impressions and fossils unearthed in the area signal a T. rex left behind the footprints roughly 66.5 million years ago. “There’s always the possibility that we haven’t found the skeletons of some species that we don’t know about,” Falkingham says. “But as far as our knowledge goes, T. rex is about the only track maker that could have made these.”
The team used stride length and body size to calculate the dinosaur’s speed. Unfortunately, the footprints aren’t well-preserved and estimating  speed from tracks is tricky, so the T. rex may have  been walking slightly faster or slower than calculated. Better tracks could have revealed whether the foot landed flat or toe-to-heel, or how foot pads supported the predator’s weight.
More tracks are sure to follow. In fact, a fifth step may be concealed in the hill. But the team is waiting for Mother Nature to wear away the surrounding rock, Hups says. “I can’t wait to get back out there and keep looking for more.”

Alzheimer’s damage may begin outside the brain

Destructive immune cells tied to Alzheimer’s disease may get their marching orders from cells outside the brain rather than within it.
In mice, suppressing a small population of immune cells located in lymph nodes protects against neurodegeneration, researchers report September 3 in Nature Neuroscience. The findings raise the possibility of treating Alzheimer’s disease while bypassing the brain’s siege defenses.
For years, researchers have gone all in on efforts to remove toxic tangles of proteins like amyloid and tau from the brain as a way of halting Alzheimer’s, with limited success. But the immune system also plays an important role in neurodegeneration. What exactly that role is — protector or antagonist — has been unclear.
In 2023, neurologist David Holtzman and colleagues showed that immune system T cells accumulate around tau tangles — implying that they might cause damage. Halting these cells’ entry into the brain reduced inflammation, and also reduced neuronal damage, says Holtzman, of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.
Still, it wasn’t known how these T cells accessed the brain in the first place. “A big question has been whether the T cells passively enter the brain or are primed … to do so,” says Rudolph Tanzi, a neurogeneticist at Harvard Medical School who wasn’t involved in the study.
During priming, T cells are ordered to rally and multiply. The generals that bark out these orders are called dendritic cells, which capture signatures of cellular threats called antigens and present them to T cell infantry.
No one had looked closely at what dendritic cells in lymph nodes were doing during neurodegenerative disease, Holtzman says. So in the new study, he and his colleagues compared two groups of mice engineered to have tau-linked neurodegeneration, one of which lacked dendritic cells.
Blocking an attack
Alzheimer’s-like neurodegeneration can ravage a brain, as seen in the slice of a mouse’s brain at left. The attack may be planned in the lymph nodes, new research suggests. The brain slice depicted on the right came from a mouse in which that early stage of attack was blocked.
Courtesy Hao Hu
In old age, mice without dendritic cells still had brains packed with tau. But compared with the other mice, they were protected against neurodegeneration and performed better on cognitive tasks like nest building.
They also had far fewer T cells in their brains. This suggests that tau tangles aren’t working alone in driving neurodegeneration, Holtzman says. “A lot of the damage that tau is causing is due to the inflammatory response that it’s eliciting.” The results would need to be replicated in human brains, he adds.
Despite this seemingly important role, the researchers found few dendritic cells in the mice’s brains. Instead, they detected threat-mimicking brain proteins traveling to the lymph nodes, where dendritic cells used them to rally T cells. The team bred mutant mice with demoted dendritic cell generals that could no longer give commands to T cells. These mice also had fewer T cells in their brains and better-preserved brain structures.
It isn’t practical to disable dendritic cells from birth in people at risk of Alzheimer’s. But Holtzman says his colleagues are working on cellular targets that could suppress them in adulthood. The real promise of the study may be a dementia treatment that bypasses the nervous system’s locked vault — the blood-brain barrier, Holtzman says. “If this panned out, potentially you wouldn’t have to get [therapeutics] into the brain.”
